findings.who: A child who files their own return and whose Alaska Permanent Fund dividend was paid to a parent, guardian, or custodian, so the child did not personally receive the check.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether you got the dividend. The child truthfully says no because the parent or custodian got it, and the gate help does not say that a payment made to someone else on the child's behalf is still the child's income.
findings.irs_text: i8814 p. 1: 'The child’s only income was from interest and dividends, including capital gain distributions and Alaska Permanent Fund dividends.' p525 p. 31: 'If you received a payment from Alaska’s mineral income fund (Alaska Permanent Fund dividend), report it as income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8g.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate and help: answer Yes if an Alaska Permanent Fund dividend was paid to the filer or to anyone on the filer's behalf, including a parent, guardian, custodian, or representative payee.

findings.who: A filer whose Alaska payment document separately shows an energy relief payment and who believes that payment is not an Alaska Permanent Fund dividend, or who received only that portion after other amounts were offset.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about an Alaska Permanent Fund dividend. The filer sees an energy relief payment and says no, not realizing the energy relief is part of the taxable dividend.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 31: 'The 2024 Alaska Permanent Fund dividend payment included an energy relief payment as part of the total dividend payment. Do not reduce the amount on line 8g by the energy relief payment portion ... the entire $1,702 ... is taxable for federal income tax purposes.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate help that an energy relief payment included in or paid with the Alaska Permanent Fund dividend counts as the dividend and must not be separated out.

findings.who: A filer who directed Alaska to pay the entire dividend to a family member, an ABLE account, or another savings vehicle not listed in the help, or whose dividend was sent to a college savings account without the filer's request.
findings.why_no: The gate help lists only debt, charity, and college savings at the filer's request. The filer reads the list as complete and says no because the payment went somewhere not listed or was not requested by the filer.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 31: 'If you received a payment from Alaska’s mineral income fund (Alaska Permanent Fund dividend), report it as income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8g.'
findings.fix: Replace the list with a general rule: answer Yes if the dividend was paid to you or to anyone else at your direction or on your behalf, regardless of where it went.

findings.who: A filer who received a late Alaska Permanent Fund dividend in 2025 that was labeled or understood as a prior year's dividend.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'In 2025' and the filer reads it as asking about the 2025 dividend. They say no because the payment was the 2024 dividend, even though they received it in 2025.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 31: 'If you received a payment from Alaska’s mineral income fund (Alaska Permanent Fund dividend), report it as income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8g.'
findings.fix: State that the year in the dividend label does not matter: answer Yes if any Alaska Permanent Fund dividend payment was received during 2025, including a late payment for an earlier year.

locators: Schedule 1 (2025), line 8g
Schedule 1 (2025), line 8g; , Alaska Permanent Fund dividend, "report it as income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8g"

findings.who: A payer under a 2016 divorce decree who must pay the mortgage or real estate tax on a home the former spouse owns or co-owns, or the premiums on a life insurance policy the former spouse owns. They make no direct cash payments to the former spouse in 2023–2025.
findings.why_no: The help mentions only rent ('Count payments made for the other person, such as rent'). The filer sees mortgage, tax or insurance payments as upkeep of property or a property-division duty, not 'support for a spouse or former spouse.' Help that also says 'a division of property' is not alimony reinforces that reading.
findings.line: s1.alimony_if_any (Schedule 1 line 19a alimony paid; line 2a for the recipient)
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 95, Line 19a: 'If you made payments to or for your spouse or former spouse under a divorce or separation agreement entered into on or before December 31, 2018, you may be able to take this deduction.'
findings.fix: Extend the help: 'Count payments the order or agreement requires you to make for the other person, such as rent, mortgage, property tax, medical bills or premiums on insurance they own, even if paid to a lender or insurer.'

findings.who: A recipient under a pre-2019 agreement whose former spouse pays cash in monthly installments called an 'equalization' or 'settlement' payment. The agreement does not say the payments are not alimony, and the payments end at the recipient's death.
findings.why_no: The help says flatly 'a division of property are not alimony,' so the filer treats any payment named as part of the settlement as outside the question, even when the cash payments may meet the alimony requirements.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 89, Line 2a: 'Enter amounts received as alimony or separate maintenance pursuant to a divorce or separation agreement entered into on or before December 31, 2018'
findings.fix: Change the help to: 'A transfer of property is not alimony. Count cash payments under the order or agreement, even if they are called part of the settlement, unless the agreement says they are not alimony; Pub. 504 explains the tests.'

findings.who: A payer under a pre-2019 decree whose payments fell after the first year, with that first year in 2023. In 2025 they owe recapture (line 2a) and paid little or nothing in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate reaches this filer only because it starts in 2023. A filer who reads the question as being about the current year ('did you pay') and paid nothing in 2025 might answer no. The words 'In 2023 or later' make that a weak misreading.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 16, Recapture of Alimony: 'If your alimony payments decrease or end during the first 3 calendar years, you may be subject to the recapture rule... you have to include in income (in the third year) part of the alimony payments you previously deducted.'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Answer Yes if any such payment was made in 2023, 2024 or 2025, even if none was made in 2025; alimony that fell or stopped can still need to be reported.'

locators: p. 89, Line 2a, "Enter amounts received as alimony or separate maintenance pursuant to a divorce or separation agreement entered into on or before December 31, 2018"; p. 95, Line 19a, "You can't take a deduction for alimony payments you made to or for your spouse if you entered into your divorce or separation agreement after December 31, 2018"; , Certain Rules for Instruments Executed or Modified After 2018, "if the modification expressly states that the alimony isn’t deductible to the payer or includible in the income of the recipient", and Example 2, "the modification expressly provided that the post-2018 alimony rules apply" and "The alimony payments made in January 2025 through May 2025 are includible in the recipient’s income and deductible from the payer’s income."
p. 89, Line 2a; p. 95, Line 19a

findings.who: A filer whose only 2025 digital-asset event was receiving new tokens from a hard fork or airdrop, and who did not sell, exchange, or receive them as payment for property or services.
findings.why_no: They read the Form 1040 digital-asset question as covering only sales/exchanges or rewards/awards/payments, so they answer No to the parent question and never reach the line 8v question.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 16 lists 'Received new digital assets as a result of a hard fork' as an example requiring 'Yes'; i1040gi p. 92 says line 8v reports ordinary income from forks, staking, or mining not reported elsewhere.
findings.fix: Ask the line 8v question even when the parent answer is No, or make the parent question/help explicitly include hard forks and airdrops and require correcting the parent to Yes.

findings.who: A filer who earned interest or lending/yield rewards in digital assets, such as from a crypto savings account or DeFi lending, and had no staking, mining, hard fork, or airdrop.
findings.why_no: The helper's examples are staking, hobby mining, hard fork, and airdrop; the filer treats that list as the whole rule and answers No because their income is interest/yield, not one of the named events.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92: 'If, in 2025, you received ordinary income in connection with digital assets that isn’t reported elsewhere on your return ... report this income on line 8v.'
findings.fix: Add interest, lending/yield rewards, referral bonuses, and other ordinary digital-asset income to the examples, or ask a broad fact question and classify after a Yes.

findings.who: A filer paid in digital assets for a one-off service and who is not in a trade or business, so the payment is neither wages nor Schedule C business income.
findings.why_no: The helper excludes 'wages, business income' and the filer thinks any payment for services must be business or wage income, so they answer No without reporting the receipt on line 8v or elsewhere.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 16: 'If you received any digital asset as compensation for services ... you must report the income as you would report other income of the same type'; p. 92 says line 8v covers ordinary digital-asset income not reported elsewhere.
findings.fix: Ask whether they received digital assets for services or property, then classify wages/business afterward; include a condition for amounts not reported on a W-2 or Schedule C.

findings.who: A filer who received staking or airdrop tokens in 2025 and later sold them at a gain, and who thinks the only taxable event is the capital gain on sale.
findings.why_no: The helper asks whether the receipt was 'ordinary income that is not ... a capital gain'; the filer knows there was a capital gain on sale and answers No, missing that the receipt itself was ordinary income.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92: line 8v covers ordinary income from staking, forks, or mining not reported elsewhere; p. 16: 'If you received ordinary income in connection with digital assets that isn’t reported elsewhere on your return, see the instructions for Schedule 1, line 8v.'
findings.fix: Ask about the receipt events themselves, such as staking, airdrop, fork, mining, or interest, without requiring the filer to decide ordinary-vs-capital; classify after a Yes.

locators: p. 15, Digital Assets, "Check the “Yes” box next to the question on digital assets on page 1 of Form 1040 or 1040-SR if at any time during 2025, you (a) received (as a reward, award, or payment for property or services)"; p. 16, "Received new digital assets as a result of mining, staking, and similar activities; • Received digital assets as a result of a hard fork"

p. 92, Line 8v, "If, in 2025, you received ordinary income in connection with digital assets that isn’t reported elsewhere on your return" and "Don’t report a gift or inheritance of digital assets on line 8v."; p. 16, How To Report Digital Asset Transactions, "If you received any digital asset as compensation for services or disposed of any digital asset that you held for sale to customers in a trade or business, you must report the income as you would report other income of the same type"
Schedule 1 (2025), line 8v; , Line 8v, "report this income on line 8v"

findings.who: A professional gambler whose winnings are all attributable to their gambling trade or business.
findings.why_no: The gate is cited to line 8b, which asks for 'gambling winnings not attributable to a trade or business.' The filer truthfully answers no because their winnings belong on Schedule C, not line 8b, so the professional-status question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 33: 'If you're in the trade or business of gambling, use Schedule C (Form 1040). For tax years 2018 through 2025, professional gambling losses and expenses are limited to the amount of your winnings.'
findings.fix: Gate on any gambling winnings before the line 8b trade-or-business exclusion, or ask the professional-status question directly; do not require positive line 8b nonbusiness winnings.

findings.who: A joint filer with no gambling winnings of their own whose spouse is a professional gambler and had gambling winnings during the year.
findings.why_no: The gate says only 'Any gambling winnings,' not 'you or your spouse'; the filer answers no for themselves, so the spouse's professional gambling business is never asked about.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 33: 'You must include your gambling winnings in your income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8b... If you're in the trade or business of gambling, use Schedule C (Form 1040).'
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you or your spouse have any gambling winnings, prizes, or awards?' and compute the gate using either spouse's winnings.

findings.who: A professional gambler with gross gambling winnings fully offset by gambling losses or expenses who reports zero or answers no because there was no net profit.
findings.why_no: They read 'Any gambling winnings' as net winnings; after offsetting losses they had none, so the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 33: 'professional gambling losses and expenses are limited to the amount of your winnings' and 'a professional gambler cannot claim a loss on Schedule C (Form 1040) in a loss year, even if gambling expenses other than losses exceed gross gambling income.'
findings.fix: Ask for gross winnings before losses/expenses, or ask 'Did you receive any gambling winnings even if you lost money overall?'

findings.who: A professional gambler in a loss year who had no gross gambling winnings, only losses or expenses, and truthfully answers no to any gambling winnings.
findings.why_no: The gate requires winnings greater than zero; with no gross winnings the truthful answer is no, so the professional-status question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 33: 'This also means that a professional gambler cannot claim a loss on Schedule C (Form 1040) in a loss year, even if gambling expenses other than losses exceed gross gambling income.'
findings.fix: Ask professional-status separately: 'Are you in the trade or business of gambling?' rather than gating it on positive winnings.

findings.who: A professional daily-fantasy-sports player who regularly and steadily makes money from fantasy contests and does not consider fantasy sports to be 'gambling.'
findings.why_no: The gate asks about 'gambling winnings'; the filer reads fantasy sports as a skill game, not gambling, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 33: 'Winnings from fantasy sports leagues are gambling winnings.' and 'If you're in the trade or business of gambling, use Schedule C (Form 1040).'
findings.fix: Name fantasy sports in the gate/help: 'gambling winnings, including fantasy sports leagues.'

findings.who: A professional gambler whose only winnings this year were noncash tournament prizes, such as a car or bonds, and who answers no because no cash was received.
findings.why_no: They read 'winnings' as cash; they received a prize, not money.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 33: 'In addition to cash winnings, you must include in your income the FMV of bonds, cars, houses, and other noncash prizes.'
findings.fix: Ask 'Any gambling winnings, prizes, or awards, including noncash prizes at fair market value?'

locators: p. 91, Line 8b
p. 33, Gambling winnings, "If you’re in the trade or business of gambling, use Schedule C (Form 1040)"

p. 33, Gambling winnings, "If you’re in the trade or business of gambling, use Schedule C (Form 1040). For tax years 2018 through 2025, professional gambling losses and expenses are limited to the amount of your winnings"

findings.who: A filer served on a jury in December 2024 and reported that jury pay on the 2024 return. The employer kept paying the salary, and the filer turned the jury pay over to the employer in January 2025. No jury pay was received in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from line 8h, which is truthfully zero for 2025 because the pay was received and reported in 2024. So the question about turning pay over to the employer is never asked, even though the repayment happened in 2025.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 34, Jury duty: "you can deduct the amount turned over to your employer as an adjustment to income. Enter the amount you repay your employer on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 24a."
findings.fix: Ask the question when line 8h > 0 OR the filer answers yes to 'In 2025, did you (or your spouse, if filing jointly) turn over to an employer any jury duty pay, including pay received in an earlier year, because the employer kept paying your salary?' Cap the answer at line 8h only for pay received in 2025.

findings.who: An employer paid full salary during jury service and later recovered the jury fee, for example by deducting it from a later paycheck or by having the court check endorsed over. The filer never handed over money directly.
findings.why_no: The question asks how much the filer did 'give to an employer'. A filer whose employer took the amount back through payroll may not see that as giving, and may answer 0 as the help text ('Give 0 if none') invites.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 34, Jury duty: "If you must give the pay to your employer because your employer continues to pay your salary ... you can deduct the amount turned over to your employer"
findings.fix: Reword as 'How much of that jury pay did you (or your spouse) turn over or repay to an employer, including amounts the employer took back from your pay or checks you signed over, because the employer kept paying your salary?'

findings.who: A filer whose employer required the jury check to be turned over regards the money as never theirs. Because they surrendered it to the employer, they leave jury pay off line 8h.
findings.why_no: The filer sees the jury pay as a pass-through, not as income. Line 8h is then zero, so the computed gate is false and line 24a is dropped. AGI nets out the same, but gross income is understated.
findings.line: s1.jury_to_employer_if_pay (Schedule 1, line 24a), together with the upstream line 8h
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 34: "Jury duty pay you receive must be included in your income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8h."
findings.fix: In the line 8h question, add help: 'Include all jury pay you or your spouse received, even if you turned it over to your employer; you can deduct the turned-over amount later.'

locators: p. 91, Line 8h, "Enter any jury duty pay and see the instructions for line 24a"; p. 99, Line 24a, "Enter your jury duty pay if you gave the pay to your employer because your employer paid your salary while you served on the jury"

p. 99, Line 24a, "Enter your jury duty pay if you gave the pay to your employer because your employer paid your salary while you served on the jury"; , Jury duty, "you can deduct the amount turned over to your employer as an adjustment to income"

findings.who: A joint filer with no Schedule C who farms on Schedule F, or rents out property on Schedule E, and uses a vehicle bought with a 2025 loan partly in that activity. They deduct part of the loan's interest on Schedule F or E.
findings.why_no: The gate counts only Schedules C. With none, the column (ii) question is never asked, and the line is fixed at zero although interest was deducted on Schedule F or E.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 110, Line 22: "enter the amount of the QPVLI, if any, that was deducted elsewhere on your return (for example, on Schedule C, Schedule E, or Schedule F)"; "you cannot deduct the same amount more than once"
findings.fix: Gate on any Schedule C, E or F (or any business or rental activity) on the return. Ask: 'How much of this loan's 2025 interest do you (or your spouse) deduct on Schedule C, E or F, for a business, farm or rental? Zero if none.'

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly. The wife runs the Schedule C business and deducts the business share of the interest on a car loan held in the husband's name or jointly. The husband is answering the interview.
findings.why_no: 'your own business' with no 'or your spouse' reads as the answering filer's business only, so he enters zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 110: "if you deducted some or all of the interest ... as interest on Schedule C ... then you can't deduct that same interest as QPVLI on Schedule 1-A"
findings.fix: 'How much of this loan's 2025 interest do you or your spouse deduct as a business expense on this return?'

findings.who: A filer with no Schedule C who has a Schedule E rental that is a trade or business, a Schedule F farm, or a partnership or S corporation K-1. In 2025 they are allowed a loss suspended in an earlier year: a passive loss freed by selling the activity, or a 704(d), 1366(d), 465 or 163(j) amount freed by new basis or at-risk amount.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed false because there is no Schedule C, so the question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i8995 p. 3: "When losses or deductions previously suspended by other Code provisions are allowed in calculating taxable income, the qualified portion ... is treated as a qualified net loss carryforward from a separate trade or business"; "Such Code provisions include ... 163(j), 179, 461(l), 465, 469, 704(d), and 1366(d)"
findings.fix: Gate on any qualified business source: Schedule C, E, or F, Form 4835, or a K-1. If none is supported, ask the question unconditionally ('any business, farm, rental or partnership/S corporation'), because the refusal is the point of the line.

findings.who: A filer whose Schedule C business closed in 2024 with a suspended passive or at-risk loss. In 2025 the loss is released and reported on Form 4797, Form 8582, or a K-1 rather than on a new Schedule C.
findings.why_no: No 2025 Schedule C, so the gate is false and the question is skipped.
findings.irs_text: i8995 p. 4, Line 3: "Include here the qualified portion of trade or business (loss) carryforward allowed in calculating taxable income in the current year, even if the loss was from a trade or business that is no longer in existence"
findings.fix: Ask whether any business ever had a loss or deduction held back that is allowed in 2025, whether or not the business still exists or files a Schedule C this year.

findings.who: A filer with a qualified business net loss from 2018 to 2024 on a return with no Form 8995 or 8995-A (for example a 2021 Schedule C or F loss). In 2025 they have no Schedule C but have QBI from a Schedule F farm, a Schedule E rental trade or business, or a K-1, or have REIT dividends that require Form 8995.
findings.why_no: The gate is false without a Schedule C. The unreported carryforward is never asked about, and Form 8995 lines 3 and 16 drop it.
findings.irs_text: i8995a p. 6: "This includes prior year loss carryforwards even if the loss was unreported or the trade or business that generated the loss is no longer in existence"; i8995 p. 5, Line 16: "This amount will offset QBI in later tax years regardless of whether the trade(s) or business(es) that generated the loss is still in existence"
findings.fix: Ask whenever the return has any QBI source or files Form 8995 or 8995-A for any reason (REIT dividends, PTP). Do not tie the question to a 2025 Schedule C.

findings.who: A filer who attached Form 8995 in 2022 only for REIT dividends and left out their Schedule C loss, so the loss was never reported.
findings.why_no: The question covers only years 'whose tax return had no Form 8995 or 8995-A'. That return had one, so the filer answers no although the loss went unreported.
findings.irs_text: i8995a p. 6, Line 6: "This amount will offset QBI in subsequent tax years regardless of whether it is reported"
findings.fix: Ask: 'In any year 2018–2024, did your or your spouse's businesses lose money overall in a year whose loss you did not carry forward on Form 8995 line 16 or Form 8995-A Schedule C line 6?'

findings.who: A filer with no Schedule C who invests in an oil and gas drilling partnership, or a partnership that publishes a periodical, and receives a K-1 reporting IDCs or circulation costs deducted in full.
findings.why_no: The gate is false without a Schedule C. Even if the question were asked, 'deduct in a business' reads as the filer's own business, not a partnership interest.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 7, Line 2t: "IDCs from oil, gas, and geothermal wells are a preference to the extent that the excess IDCs are more than 65% of the net income from the wells"; Line 2o: circulation costs "deducted in full for the regular tax ... must be capitalized and amortized over 3 years for the AMT"
findings.fix: Ask unconditionally, or whenever a Schedule C, E, or F or a K-1 is present: 'Did you or your spouse, directly or through a partnership, S corporation, estate or trust, deduct ...'

findings.who: A filer who in 2023 or 2024 deducted in full circulation costs or mining exploration and development costs in a Schedule C business that has since closed, or that incurred no such costs in 2025.
findings.why_no: With no 2025 Schedule C the gate is false. With one, 'Do you ... deduct' in the present tense gets a no because nothing was deducted in 2025. Yet the 3-year or 10-year AMT amortization still gives a 2025 AMT deduction, a negative adjustment.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 7, Line 2q: "Mining exploration and development costs deducted in full for the regular tax in the tax year they were paid or incurred must be capitalized and amortized over 10 years for the AMT"; "If the AMT deduction is more than the regular tax deduction, enter the difference as a negative amount"
findings.fix: Add 'in 2025 or any of the 9 earlier years (3 for periodical costs), including in a business you no longer run', and do not gate on a 2025 Schedule C.

findings.who: An author or film owner with no Schedule C who reports royalties on Schedule E and depreciates the property under the income forecast method. 2025 is the 3rd or 10th year after it was placed in service. Or a partner or S corporation shareholder whose entity completed a long-term contract in 2025 and passes the look-back computation to the owners.
findings.why_no: The gate is false without a Schedule C, so Form 8866 and Form 8697 are never asked about.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 Schedule 2 (2025), line 17n: "Look-back interest under section 167(g) or 460(b) from Form 8697 or 8866"
findings.fix: Ask unconditionally, noting a Schedule E royalty property or a K-1 from an entity with long-term contracts.

findings.who: A contractor whose Schedule C business ended in 2024 after finishing a long-term contract. The contract price or costs were adjusted in 2025.
findings.why_no: No 2025 Schedule C, so the question is skipped, although a post-completion adjustment in 2025 triggers look-back interest.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 7, Line 2p Note: "you may owe or be entitled to a refund of interest for the tax year the contract is completed or adjusted. For details, see Form 8697"
findings.fix: Do not gate on a current Schedule C. Say 'including a business you no longer run'.

findings.who: A filer with farm income on Schedule F or Form 4835 (a crop-share landlord under a written lease) and no Schedule C. Or a fishing-vessel lessor paid a share of the catch who reports on Schedule E.
findings.why_no: The gate counts only Schedules C, and the question names only fishing. Farming income, which Schedule J also covers, is never offered.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 36: "If you had income from farming or fishing, your tax may be less if you choose to figure it using income averaging on Schedule J"; i1040sj p. 1: farming business includes "Leasing land to a tenant engaged in a farming business" on a share basis
findings.fix: Gate on Schedule C, F, Form 4835, Schedule E, or a K-1. Ask: 'Do you or your spouse have income from a farming or fishing business and choose to average it (Schedule J)?'

findings.who: A general partner with self-employment income on a K-1, or a farmer filing Schedule F, with no Schedule C, who contributes to the partnership's Keogh or 401(k) or to a solo 401(k) for 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate is false without a Schedule C, so the plan question is never asked. The Schedule 1 line 16 deduction is dropped and the refusal is missed.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 93, Line 16: "If you were self-employed or a partner, you may be able to take this deduction"
findings.fix: Gate on any self-employment income (Schedule SE, Schedule F, or K-1 box 14). Ask: '...a retirement plan of your own business or of a partnership you are a partner in...'

findings.who: A filer operates a farm mostly for recreation and pleasure and receives income from selling crops, livestock, or farm products; they do not consider it a hobby.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about a 'hobby (not a business).' A recreation-and-pleasure farm is not a hobby in ordinary wording, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 31: An example of this type of activity is a hobby or a farm you operate mostly for recreation and pleasure. Enter this income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8j.
findings.fix: Ask about money or goods from any activity not engaged in for profit, expressly including a hobby or a farm operated mostly for recreation or pleasure, even if no profit was expected.

findings.who: A filer runs an unprofitable activity they label a business—for example, horse boarding, craft sales, or an LLC—and receives gross receipts but does not expect to make a profit.
findings.why_no: They read 'hobby (not a business)' as requiring them to classify the activity, answer no because they believe it is a business, and never report the gross receipts on line 8j.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 31: You must include on your return income from an activity, even if you don’t expect to make a profit from that activity. An example of this type of activity is a hobby or a farm you operate mostly for recreation and pleasure. Enter this income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8j.
findings.fix: Do not ask the filer to self-classify as hobby versus business; ask whether they received gross receipts from any activity in which they did not expect a profit, and classify after a broad yes. State that an LLC or business label is not controlling.

findings.who: A filer regularly buys and sells old gear as a hobby, not for personal use, does not expect a profit, and receives money from those sales.
findings.why_no: The help says selling things you owned for your own use, such as a collection or old gear, is not this. The filer reads 'old gear' as excluding all old-gear sales and answers no.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 31: You must include on your return income from an activity, even if you don’t expect to make a profit from that activity. An example of this type of activity is a hobby or a farm you operate mostly for recreation and pleasure. Enter this income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8j.
findings.fix: Limit the help to personal-use property actually held for the filer’s own use, and state that gross receipts from a hobby of buying, restoring, or dealing in goods are not excluded merely because the goods are old gear or collectibles.

locators: Schedule 1 (2025), line 8j

p. 91, Line 8j, "Activity not engaged in for profit income. See Pub. 525"; , Activity not for profit, "An example of this type of activity is a hobby or a farm you operate mostly for recreation and pleasure. Enter this income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8j"

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly in 2025. In 2023 one spouse had a Schedule C loss larger than all other income, and the prior return showed negative taxable income. They never filed Form 172 or used the words 'net operating loss.' They married in 2024.
findings.why_no: The helper asks whether they are carrying a loss 'as a net operating loss deduction.' They do not know whether their loss is an NOL, so they answer no. The gated question is never asked, and the deduction against the joint income is never limited.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3, Change in Marital Status: "If you and your spouse were not married to each other in all years involved in figuring NOL carrybacks and carryovers, only the spouse who had the loss can take the NOL deduction."
findings.fix: Ask a fact the filer can check first: 'Did you or your spouse have a year since 2018 in which losses or deductions were more than income (negative taxable income, a Form 172, or an NOL deduction on Schedule 1)?' Classify the NOL after a broad yes.

findings.who: A joint filer whose 2024 business losses exceeded the excess business loss limit (Form 461). The disallowed amount carries into 2025 as an NOL. The filer married the current spouse in 2025.
findings.why_no: The filer thinks of the amount as an 'excess business loss' carryover, not a 'net operating loss.' The helper's list of business, farm, rental and disaster losses does not name it.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3, Change in Marital Status: "only the spouse who had the loss can take the NOL deduction. If you file a joint return, the NOL deduction is limited to the income of that spouse"
findings.fix: Add to the helper's help: 'This includes an excess business loss disallowed on Form 461 in an earlier year, an NOL passed to you from a terminated estate or trust, and ordinary losses on small business (section 1244) stock.'

findings.who: A joint filer who, before the current marriage, had an ordinary loss on small business (section 1244) stock. The loss created an NOL that still carries into 2025.
findings.why_no: The helper says 'not a capital loss from selling investments.' Selling stock sounds like selling investments, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3, Change in Marital Status: "only the spouse who had the loss can take the NOL deduction"
findings.fix: Reword the exclusion: 'not a capital loss carryover (Schedule D). An ordinary loss on small business stock does count.'

findings.who: A spouse who received an NOL carryover from a terminated estate or trust in which they were a beneficiary (excess deductions in the final year). The filer married the current spouse after that year.
findings.why_no: The helper asks about a loss 'you (or your spouse)' had from a business, farm, rental or disaster. A carryover passed through from an estate does not feel like the filer's own loss of any listed kind.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3, Change in Marital Status: "If you file a joint return, the NOL deduction is limited to the income of that spouse."
findings.fix: Name in the helper's help: 'an NOL carryover passed to you from an estate or trust that ended.'

findings.who: A joint couple who married each other, divorced in 2021, and remarried each other in 2023. One spouse's 2019 farm NOL still carries into 2025.
findings.why_no: They were married to each other in 2019, when the loss arose, and are married now. They read the question as asking about the loss year and the present, overlooking the gap years in between, and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3, Change in Marital Status: "not married to each other in all years involved in figuring NOL carrybacks and carryovers"
findings.fix: Ask positively and year by year: 'Were you and your spouse married to each other at the end of every year from the year the loss arose (and any year it was carried back to) through 2025?' A No ends the interview.

findings.who: A joint couple, married to each other since 2017. One spouse's 2020 NOL was carried back five years under the 2018–2020 rule to 2015, before they married, and the rest carries into 2025.
findings.why_no: They focus on the year the loss arose and on the years since, both of which fall inside the marriage. They miss that a carryback year falls before the marriage.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3, Change in Marital Status: "all years involved in figuring NOL carrybacks and carryovers"
findings.fix: State in the help: 'Include any earlier year the loss was carried back to, such as up to 5 years back for 2018–2020 losses or 2 years back for farm losses.'

findings.who: Any joint filer facing the gated question.
findings.why_no: The double negative 'Were you … not married to each other' invites a reversed answer. A couple with an unmarried year in the loss period can answer no, meaning 'we were married,' and lose the refusal.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3, Change in Marital Status: "If you and your spouse were not married to each other in all years involved"
findings.fix: Remove the negation: 'Were you and your spouse married to each other in every one of those years?' Treat a No as the refusal condition.

findings.who: A filer now filing single, head of household or married filing separately whose 2023 joint return showed an NOL. Both spouses had losses that year, but the larger one came from the other spouse's business. Under the allocation, part of the joint NOL is this filer's share and carries into 2025.
findings.why_no: On a return that is not joint, the scope helper asks only about 'you'. The filer thinks of the loss as the spouse's or ex-spouse's business loss, or as the couple's joint loss, not 'a loss you are carrying'. So they answer no, and the joint-history question that ends the interview is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3, Joint to separate returns: 'figure each of your carryovers separately by separating the NOL portion for each spouse from within the joint return ... If both spouses have an NOL, multiply the joint NOL by a fraction ... The rest of the joint NOL is spouse B's share.'
findings.fix: Ask the joint-history fact first and broadly: 'Did you, or a joint return you signed with any spouse, have a business, farm, rental or disaster loss in an earlier year that was more than the income on that return, and not all used up by 2024?' On a return that is not joint, treat any loss shown on an earlier joint return as possibly partly yours.

findings.who: A filer who in an earlier year sold, or found worthless, stock in a small corporation they helped found (section 1244 stock), with an ordinary loss that created an NOL. They filed jointly in that year and file separately or single now.
findings.why_no: The helper excludes 'a capital loss from selling investments'. A stock sale reads to the filer as exactly that, so they answer no, though a section 1244 loss is an ordinary, business-type loss that can produce an NOL.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3, Joint to separate returns: 'If you and your spouse file separate returns for a tax year, but filed a joint return for any or all of the tax years involved in figuring the NOL carryover, figure each of your carryovers separately'
findings.fix: Ask about a checkable fact: 'Did an earlier return, yours or a joint one, show a negative total after deductions, or a Form 172 or NOL carryover worksheet, that is not used up?' Add help naming small business (section 1244) stock, worthless business stock, K-1 losses and sales of business property as possible sources.

findings.who: A filer whose earlier-year NOL came from a K-1 loss passed through from a partnership or S corporation, or from a section 1231 loss on selling business equipment or rental property. The loss arose on a joint return, and the filer now files separately.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'business, farm, rental or disaster loss' as their own sole proprietorship, farm, or rental activity, not as a passive-investor K-1 or the sale of property. They also do not recognize the carryover as an 'NOL deduction' because a prior preparer computed it. So they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3, Deducting a Carryforward: 'If you carry forward your NOL to a tax year after the NOL year, list your NOL deduction as a negative figure on Schedule 1 (Form 1040)'; Joint to separate returns: 'figure each of your carryovers separately'
findings.fix: Have the help point to evidence: 'Look at your 2024 Schedule 1 line 8a, or for a Form 172 or an NOL carryover statement with your prior returns. Losses from partnerships, S corporations and the sale of business property count.'

findings.who: A graduate student receives a fellowship or grant that requires teaching, dorm supervision, or other work; the stipend is not reported on a W-2.
findings.why_no: They read 'for study or research' as covering only academic study or research, not pay for teaching or other required work, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 35, Payment for services: 'Generally, you can’t exclude from your gross income the part of any scholarship or fellowship that represents payment for teaching, research, or other services required as a condition for receiving the scholarship'.
findings.fix: Ask about any scholarship, fellowship, grant, stipend, or living allowance not on a W-2, and expressly include pay for teaching, research, or other work the grant required; don't limit the gate to study or research.

findings.who: A student athlete receives an athletic scholarship covering room and board, or a student receives a service or leadership scholarship for room and board, and no part is on a W-2.
findings.why_no: They read 'for study or research' as requiring an academic study or research purpose, so they answer no because the award was for athletics or service.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92, Line 8r: 'if you were a degree candidate, include on line 8r only the amounts you used for expenses other than tuition and course-related expenses. For example, amounts used for room, board, and travel must be reported on line 8r'; p525 p. 35: 'Amounts used for room and board don’t qualify for the exclusion.'
findings.fix: Remove the 'for study or research' limitation; ask about any scholarship, fellowship, grant, stipend, or living allowance, including athletic, service, or other non-academic awards, not reported on a W-2.

findings.who: A student's scholarship provider pays the student's landlord directly for housing; the student receives no cash and no W-2.
findings.why_no: The help says to count grants 'paid to you or straight to the school,' and they read that list as exhaustive, so they answer no because the payment went to the landlord.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92, Line 8r: 'amounts used for room, board, and travel must be reported on line 8r'; p525 p. 35: 'Amounts used for room and board don’t qualify for the exclusion.'
findings.fix: Say the grant can be paid to the filer, to the school, or to any other person on the filer's behalf; ask whether any scholarship or grant was used for room, board, travel, or other non-tuition costs.

findings.who: A degree candidate receives a grant with a non-W-2 room-and-board portion plus a separate teaching stipend reported on a W-2; they focus on the W-2 and answer no.
findings.why_no: They read 'not on a W-2' as asking whether the award was reported on a W-2 at all, not whether any portion was not on a W-2.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92, Line 8r: 'Enter the amount of scholarship and fellowship grants not reported on Form W-2. However, if you were a degree candidate, include on line 8r only the amounts you used for expenses other than tuition and course-related expenses.'
findings.fix: Ask whether any part of the scholarship or fellowship was not reported on a W-2, even if another part was reported on a W-2; clarify that W-2 amounts are excluded but non-W-2 room and board is not.

findings.who: A filer exercised incentive stock options in 2024 and sold the shares in 2025 before the holding period ended, creating a 2025 disqualifying-disposition ordinary income amount not reported in W-2 box 1.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether they exercised employee stock options in 2025. They truthfully answer no because the exercise was in 2024, even though the 2025 sale produces stock-option income reportable on Schedule 1 line 8k.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8k: 'Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1h'; f1040s1 line 8k is 'Stock options.'
findings.fix: Ask whether in 2025 they exercised stock options OR sold or otherwise disposed of shares acquired by exercising stock options, including a disqualifying disposition of ISO or ESPP shares, and then ask for the option-related income not in W-2 box 1.

findings.who: A nonemployee director, consultant, or other service provider exercised nonstatutory stock options in 2025 for services, received no W-2, and has option spread not reported on Form 1040 line 1h.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about 'employee stock options.' They are not an employee, so they truthfully answer no, though the IRS line says any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported on line 1h.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8k: 'Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1h'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to stock options, including options received for services as a nonemployee as well as options inherited or received in a divorce, and ask for the amount not in W-2 box 1.

findings.who: A filer exercised nonstatutory employee stock options in 2025 and held the shares; the bargain element was not included in W-2 box 1, and the filer received no cash from a sale.
findings.why_no: The second helper asks whether they had 'income' from the exercise. Seeing no sale and no cash, they answer no, even though the excess of the stock's value when exercised over the option price is income from the exercise.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8k: 'Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1h'
findings.fix: Ask whether the value of the stock when exercised was more than the amount paid for the option, even if no shares were sold and no cash was received; then subtract any amount included in W-2 box 1.

locators: p. 91, Line 8k, "Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1h"
Schedule 1 (2025), line 8k; , Line 8k, "Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1h"

findings.who: A filer (or spouse) who was collecting unemployment, then became ill or injured. In 2025 they received government disability payments from a state disability program, paid in place of the unemployment benefits they could no longer draw.
findings.why_no: The question asks about 'unemployment benefits' or 'paid family leave'. What they received was a disability benefit, so they truthfully answer no. The help mentions Form 1099-G box 1, but they may never open the online-only form, and they may not link a disability payment to it.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 29: unemployment compensation includes '• Disability payments from a government program paid as a substitute for unemployment compensation.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate: '...or government disability payments you received instead of unemployment benefits (for example, after you became unable to work while unemployed)?' Add to the help: 'Workers' compensation does not count.'

findings.who: A railroad worker (or spouse) who received railroad unemployment benefits from the Railroad Retirement Board in 2025.
findings.why_no: The words 'a government (such as a state's)' and the stress on state programs can suggest that only state unemployment insurance counts. A railroad worker may treat RRB payments as a separate federal railroad benefit and not as 'unemployment benefits'.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 29: unemployment compensation includes '• Railroad unemployment compensation benefits.'
findings.fix: In the help, list the federal programs: 'including railroad unemployment benefits from the Railroad Retirement Board, Disaster Unemployment Assistance, and Airline Deregulation Act unemployment assistance.'

findings.who: A filer who received Disaster Unemployment Assistance after a federally declared disaster, or a self-employed person paid under such a program, while not eligible for regular state unemployment insurance.
findings.why_no: They may see the payment as disaster relief, which is often tax-free, and not as 'unemployment benefits', especially since they were told they did not qualify for regular unemployment.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 29: '• Unemployment assistance under the Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act of 1974'; 'Unemployment assistance payments under the Act are taxable unemployment compensation.'
findings.fix: Name Disaster Unemployment Assistance in the help, and say it counts even though disaster relief grants usually do not.

findings.who: A filer in a state that brands its program differently, for example 'Reemployment Assistance' or 'Family Leave Insurance' paid by a state disability or labor agency.
findings.why_no: The program name they know does not contain 'unemployment' or 'paid family leave', so they may not recognize it in the question.
findings.irs_text: f1099g p. 5, Box 1: 'If you made contributions to a governmental UC program or to a governmental paid family leave program and received a payment from that program, the payer must issue a separate Form 1099-G'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Your state may call it reemployment assistance, jobless benefits, or family leave insurance.'

locators: p. 89, Schedule 1, line 7

p. 89, Schedule 1, line 7, 'You should receive a Form 1099-G showing in box 1 the total unemployment compensation paid to you in 2025' and 'If the amount reported in box 1 of your Form(s) 1099-G is incorrect, report on line 7 only the actual amount'

findings.who: A filer receives a payment designated as interest on unpaid lottery installments in 2025, with no current principal installment.
findings.why_no: The gate asks for gambling or lottery winnings; the help mentions yearly lottery installments and sales of future payments, not interest, so the filer says no because it is only interest.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 33: if you win a state lottery prize payable in installments, include the annual payments and any amounts you receive designated as interest on the unpaid installments.
findings.fix: Add interest on unpaid lottery installments to the gate, or ask whether the filer received any lottery-related payment including interest.

findings.who: A salesperson is awarded prize points by a distributor or manufacturer in 2025 that are made available for redemption but are not redeemed until later.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether the filer received a prize or award; the filer has only been credited points and has not received merchandise, so answers no.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 35: the prize points are taxable in the year they're paid or made available to you, rather than in the year you redeem them for merchandise.
findings.fix: Mention prize points made available in the gate, or ask whether the filer was awarded or credited prize points usable in 2025.

findings.who: A filer won money in a fantasy sports league and regards fantasy sports as a skill contest, not gambling.
findings.why_no: The gate says gambling or lottery winnings; its help does not mention fantasy sports, so the filer answers no rather than classifying the league as gambling.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 33: Winnings from fantasy sports leagues are gambling winnings.
findings.fix: Add fantasy sports winnings explicitly to the gate.

findings.who: A filer wins a contest prize consisting of services, such as a spa package or a free tour, rather than goods.
findings.why_no: The gate help says prizes in goods; the filer reads that as limiting noncash prizes to goods and answers no for a service prize.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 35: Prizes and awards in goods or services must be included in your income at their FMV.
findings.fix: Change the gate help to say prizes in goods or services.

findings.who: An Olympic or Paralympic medalist received a medal, and possibly no separate USOC prize money, in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks for gambling or lottery winnings or a prize or award, but its help lists lottery installments, sales, and goods; the filer does not read an Olympic medal as a prize or award and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, line 8m: The value of Olympic and Paralympic medals and the amount of USOC prize money you receive on account of your participation in the Olympic or Paralympic Games may be nontaxable.
findings.fix: Add Olympic and Paralympic medals and USOC prize money explicitly to the gate, before the special line that ends the interview.
